analysis.one_liner: Restores strict flammability standards for children's sleepwear that regulators had loosened in 1996.
analysis.headline: A bill to restore strict flammability rules for children's sleepwear died in a House committee without a single hearing or vote, despite 38 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1996, the Consumer Product Safety Commission loosened the federal flammability rules for children's sleepwear, allowing snug-fitting cotton garments to be sold without meeting the old burn standards. This bill would have ordered the Commission to revoke that 1996 change and put the stricter rules back in place for sizes 0 through 14. It was introduced in May 1998, referred to the House Commerce Committee and a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children, who would face a lower risk of burn injuries from sleepwear that can catch fire; the stricter standards applied to all children's sleepwear sold in the U.S., sizes 0 through 14.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the CPSC to issue a rule revoking the September 9, 1996 amendments that loosened the flammability standards for children's sleepwear sizes 0 through 6X and 7 through 14, restoring the stricter burn requirements. [S3]
It sets a deadline: the Commission must propose the rule within 90 days of enactment and issue a final rule within 270 days, preventing indefinite delay. [S3]
Sleepwear already manufactured or imported under the looser rules would not be recalled or penalized, so the change would apply going forward. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of untreated cotton and snug-fitting sleepwear, which would have to meet strict flammability tests again or switch to flame-resistant fabrics, with likely higher prices and fewer style choices for parents.

drawbacks.text: The bill strips away the normal rules that govern federal regulation: it declares that no statute or Executive order — including the Administrative Procedure Act's public comment process, environmental review, and small-business impact analysis — applies to the rule it orders. That means the stricter standard would be reinstated without the usual opportunity for manufacturers, retailers, or the public to weigh in. [S3]

The CPSC adopted the 1996 loosening through its own safety analysis, concluding that snug-fitting garments and certain infant sizes could meet the safety goal without the old requirements; the bill substitutes Congress's judgment for the regulator's on a technical safety question. [S3]
Requiring flame-resistant fabrics or treated materials can raise the cost of children's sleepwear, a cost that falls on families buying clothes for growing kids. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real: strict flammability standards reduce burn injuries to children, while the loosened 1996 rules gave parents cheaper, more natural-fiber options. The bill's biggest design flaw is procedural — it forces the stricter standard through without any public comment or regulatory analysis, trading process for speed. A bill with the same goal that followed normal rulemaking would have been easier to defend.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Commerce Committee, which passed it along to a subcommittee, and it sat there until Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and no action.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the Children's Sleepwear Safety Act of 1998 on May 12, 1998, joined by Reps. Rosa DeLauro and Curt Weldon of Pennsylvania. [S3]
The bill drew 38 cosponsors — 33 Democrats and 5 Republicans. [S4]
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce the day it was introduced, and two weeks later, on May 26, 1998, to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection. [S5]
That was the last action of any kind; the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of snug-fitting, untreated sleepwear — and the looser 1996 standard they operate under — were better off, because the stricter rules were never restored. Families gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate strict children's sleepwear flammability standards.

for.name: Reps. Rosa DeLauro and Curt Weldon
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction on day one, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: 38 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of restoring the stricter flammability standards.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the eight months before the Congress ended.

against.name: Snug-fitting sleepwear manufacturers
against.role: Industry benefiting from the 1996 loosened standard
against.what_they_did: Benefited from the flammability exemption the bill sought to repeal; the 1996 rule change followed a manufacturer petition, and the industry had a direct financial stake in the committee not acting.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic (33 of 38 cosponsors) but included 5 Republicans, and no vote was ever taken on the merits.

industries.industry: Snug-fitting and untreated cotton sleepwear manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would have repealed the 1996 exemption that lets these garments be sold without meeting strict flammability tests, forcing redesign, treated fabrics, or higher prices. Their cheaper product would no longer meet the standard for children's sleepwear.
Restoring the strict standards would push sales back toward garments made of flame-resistant materials, reversing the market shift the 1996 rule created.
Retailers would face a smaller, more regulated product range and compliance costs, but also lower liability exposure from flammable sleepwear.
